The New Sociology of Science as the Foundation of the Epistemic Process: A Coherence–Persistence Rereading of Auguste Comte
Authors/Creators
Kriger, Boris
Description
The canonical reading of Auguste Comte places sociology at the apex of a hierarchical classification of the sciences, understood as the terminal discipline because it is the most complex and the most dependent on its predecessors. This paper argues that the canonical reading misidentifies the structural role sociology plays in Comte’s system. A careful rereading, combined with a formal framework developed in recent work on coherence and structural persistence, supports an alternative thesis: sociology is not the apex of the epistemic ladder but its
foundation
—the instance that determines, for any given community, which claims will be treated as real and which will be ignored and erased. Correctness plays only a secondary role in this determination; coherence plays a substantial one, and the coherence-persistence framework adopted here explains both facts. Knowledge without social persistence is not knowledge in any scientifically tractable sense; it is a private cognitive state structurally indistinguishable, at the level of collective inquiry, from the absence of that state. We formalize this intuition by modeling scientific knowledge as a persistent structure across a composite system comprising the individual, the stabilizing artifacts, the community, and the transmission channels, and by proving a Social Indistinguishability Theorem: in the absence of social persistence, the likelihood ratio between “the agent knows
” and “the agent does not know
” converges to unity for any external epistemic observer. A corollary gives the paper its slogan:
a thrice-Einstein without community is indistinguishable from a non-Einstein
. The result is then used to diagnose several open problems in contemporary philosophy of science and philosophy of mind, including the stalemate in scientific realism, the structural prospects of artificial agents as epistemic carriers, and the ongoing dispute concerning the scientific status of the concept of consciousness. Philipp N. Herrmann Dennis O. Kundisch 
University of Paderborn University of Paderborn

Mohammad S. Rahman1

mohammad.rahman@haskayne.ucalgary.ca 
 
Working Paper 
April 2012 
Abstract 
In this research, we investigate the impact of delegating decision making to information technology (IT) 
on an important human decision bias – the sunk cost effect. To address our research question, we use a 
unique and very rich dataset containing actual market tr ansaction data for approximately 7,000 pay -per-
bid auctions. Thus, unlike previous studies that are primarily laboratory experiments, we investigate the 
effects of using IT on the proneness to a decision bias in real market transactions. We identify and 
analyze irrational decision scenarios of auction participants . We find that  participants with a higher 
monetary investment have an increased likelihood of violating the assumption of rationality , due to the 
sunk cost effect. Interestingly, after controlling for monetary investments, participants who delegate their 
decision making to IT and, consequently, have comparably lower behavioral investments (e.g., emotional 
attachment, effort, time) are less prone to the sunk cost effect. In particular, delegation to IT reduces the 
impact of overall investments on the sunk cost effect by approximately 50%.  
Keywords: Internet Markets, Delegating to IT, S unk Cost Effect, Economics of Automated Agents, 
Decision Support Systems, Decision Bias.
